rules_evaluated.rule_lead: Heading grammar is the mood switch, and it is load-bearing.
rules_evaluated.evidence: Harm checked: an imperative heading inside a lecture blurs the grammar split that lets a declarative EXERCISE heading register as a law. Chunk 5's header 'Keep your context where it loads optimally' (L39) is imperative-mood ('Keep...'), structurally identical to the rule's own exercise example ('Read the ticket for your bug'), unlike this file's other four headers which are all declarative claims ('Rules have a ceiling', 'Prohibitions stop; taste steers'). It does not fit the rule's named NOT-violation shapes (orientation header, catalogue entry naming a subject, phase/section label inside a walk). Checked the maintainer block before scoring: raw L52 names this exact heading and its placement as a direct maintainer call ('The lecture closes on *Keep your context where it loads optimally* (Antti-directed 2026-08-23; reordered to last the same day...)'), so the wording is authored intent, not generation drift, and the comprehension harm the rule guards against is not actually present -- a reader is not misled into treating this as a mandatory task; the body around it is explicit that the prompt is optional ('run it on your own files whenever you like', L44). Scored PASS rather than REVISE per the preamble's harm test, applying this class's own severity principle (an imperative lecture heading is a mood-consistency tell, not an 'I cannot follow this' failure) -- filed as a TODO below rather than a gate.
